summary: This note is a research article reporting a large-scale observational study of littering behavior across 130 outdoor public locations in the United States, with 9,757 individuals observed. It covers general littering of any item (17% of disposals resulted in litter) and a separate smoker sample where the cigarette butt littering rate was 65%. Multilevel modeling found age and gender predicted individual littering, while existing litter and fewer trash receptacles predicted site-level littering; distance from a receptacle also predicted littering. The note includes the literature review, methods, and results, and it is cut off partway through the receptacle analysis.
one_line: Field study of 9,757 observed individuals at 130 US public sites finding that 17% of disposals were littered, with age, existing litter and receptacle availability as predictors.
key_facts: The study observed coded littering behavior among 9,757 individuals at 130 outdoor public locations in the United States.
For smokers, the observed littering rate for cigarette butts was 65%.
Of all disposal behaviors observed, 17% resulted in litter.
Multilevel modeling showed that age (negatively) was predictive of individual littering.
At the site level, the presence of existing litter (positively) and the availability of trash receptacles (negatively) predicted littering.
Among individuals who disposed of an item, distance to the receptacle was positively predictive of littering.
The observations were conducted in spring 2008 across 10 states: Arkansas, California, Georgia, Illinois, Kentucky, Nevada, New Mexico, New York, Utah, and Vermont.
Of the 8,990 general observations, 2,472 people left with no object (28%), 4,534 left with an object (50%), and 1,962 disposed of an object on site (22%).
Among the 1,962 disposals, 342 instances of littering were observed, and cigarettes were the most frequent disposed object (N = 340).
The mean distance to a receptacle at the time of littering was 29 feet.
Observations of each site continued until 30 participants were observed making a disposal or until an 8-hour observation period concluded, with a minimum of 4 hours at each site.
The article cites an estimated direct litter cleanup cost of conservatively more than US$11 billion annually in the United States (MSW Consultants, 2009).
In the general littering observations, men (21%) littered more than women (15%), and the 18 to 29 age group littered at 26%.
